source_content.content: ### 5.1 Setup #### Datasets We evaluate AutoSearch on six widely used QA datasets, divided into two categories. (1) General QA: NQ*Kwiatkowski et al. ([2019](#bib.bib31 "Natural questions: a benchmark for question answering research"))*, TriviaQA*Joshi et al. ([2017](#bib.bib32 "Triviaqa: a large scale distantly supervised challenge dataset for reading comprehension"))*, and PopQA*Mallen et al. ([2023](#bib.bib33 "When not to trust language models: investigating effectiveness and limitations of parametric and non-parametric memories"))*; (2) Multi-hop QA: HotpotQA*Yang et al. ([2018](#bib.bib34 "HotpotQA: a dataset for diverse, explainable multi-hop question answering"))*, 2WikiMultiHopQA*Ho et al. ([2020](#bib.bib35 "Constructing a multi-hop qa dataset for comprehensive evaluation of reasoning steps"))*, and Bamboogle*Press et al. ([2023](#bib.bib37 "Measuring and narrowing the compositionality gap in language models"))*. These datasets cover a broad spectrum of scenarios, allowing a comprehensive evaluation of AutoSearch. #### Baselines We compare AutoSearch against several RL-based search baselines, including Search-R1*Jin et al. ([2025](#bib.bib17 "Search-r1: training llms to reason and leverage search engines with reinforcement learning"))*, StepSearch*Zheng et al. ([2025](#bib.bib19 "StepSearch: igniting llms search ability via step-wise proximal policy optimization"))*, and HiPRAG*Wu et al. ([2026](#bib.bib23 "HiPRAG: hierarchical process rewards for efficient agentic retrieval augmented generation"))*. #### Evaluation Metrics We assess answer quality using the canonical Exact Match (EM) and word-level F1 scores. To evaluate search cost and efficiency, we report Search Depth (SD), which records the number of search steps, and Search Efficiency (SE) ($\text{SE}\=\text{EM}/\text{SD}$), quantifying the accuracy gained per search step. We also introduce the Over-Searching Ratio (OSR), the proportion of samples correctly answered before the final search step, to quantify over-searching. *Table 2: Over-Searching Ratio (OSR% $\downarrow$) Comparison.* | Method | General QA | | | Multi-Hop QA | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | NQ | Tri. | Pop. | Hot. | 2Wi. | Bam. | | \rowcolorpurple!10 Base model: Qwen2.5-3b-Base/Instruct | | | | | | | | Search-R1-base | 3.50 | 2.10 | 5.60 | 9.20 | 11.1 | 6.50 | | Search-R1-instruct | 8.70 | 3.90 | 8.90 | 13.9 | 11.3 | 16.9 | | StepSearch-base | 25.2 | 12.2 | 27.7 | 33.9 | 32.4 | 37.1 | | StepSearch-instruct | 5.70 | 4.30 | 4.90 | 18.1 | 12.7 | 15.3 | | HIPRAG-base | 2.70 | 1.80 | 5.50 | 2.60 | 0.80 | 3.20 | | HIPRAG-instruct | 0.70 | 0.80 | 1.80 | 1.70 | 1.40 | 3.20 | | \rowcolororange!10 AutoSearch | 0.00 | 0.10 | 0.00 | 0.90 | 2.60 | 2.40 | | \rowcolorpurple!10 Base model: Qwen2.5-7b-Base/Instruct | | | | | | | | Search-R1-base | 13.0 | 6.50 | 11.4 | 32.4 | 32.3 | 30.6 | | Search-R1-instruct | 9.30 | 3.90 | 6.80 | 23.4 | 27.2 | 29.8 | | StepSearch-base | 12.2 | 7.10 | 12.1 | 23.8 | 24.5 | 29.0 | | StepSearch-instruct | 20.8 | 10.9 | 26.6 | 27.3 | 26.4 | 32.3 | | HIPRAG-instruct | 4.50 | 2.20 | 7.90 | 12.5 | 18.9 | 11.3 | | \rowcolororange!10 AutoSearch | 1.83 | 0.51 | 0.50 | 5.78 | 8.52 | 10.1 | #### Training and Evaluation We conduct experiments on two models from the Qwen series: Qwen-2.5-3B-Base and Qwen-2.5-7B-Base. Following Search-R1, we merge the training sets of NQ and HotpotQA dataset to form training corpus. During training, the retrieval module used the 2018 Wikipedia snapshot*Karpukhin et al. ([2020](#bib.bib38 "Dense passage retrieval for open-domain question answering"))* with the E5 retriever*Wang et al. ([2022](#bib.bib39 "Text embeddings by weakly-supervised contrastive pre-training"))*, uniformly sampling $k\=3$ documents. To ensure fair and reproducible comparisons, we independently reproduce the results of baseline methods. ### 5.2 Main Results AutoSearch Achieves Superior Performance. Table[4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2 "Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning") reports the performance of AutoSearch and baseline methods across six QA datasets. Across both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, as well as single-hop and multi-hop QA tasks, AutoSearch consistently outperforms the baselines, achieving higher EM and F1 scores and demonstrating robust accuracy across diverse scenarios. AutoSearch Balances Accuracy and Efficiency. The search depth results show that Search-R1 and StepSearch achieve strong answer accuracy but rely on deeper searches, resulting in higher computational cost. In contrast, HiPRAG adopts fewer search depth on most tasks, which reduces search cost but leads to noticeably lower accuracy. Compared to baselines, AutoSearch consistently achieves higher accuracy with fewer search steps across most tasks, demonstrating balanced trade-off between answer accuracy and search efficiency. AutoSearch Adaptively Adjusts Search Depth. AutoSearch does not simply minimize search depth. On single-hop datasets, it maintains relatively shallow searches, while on multi-hop datasets, it performs noticeably more search steps. The search efficiency metric shows that, compared to baseline methods, AutoSearch achieves higher efficiency across most datasets, indicating its ability to adaptively adjust search depth based on question complexity and the agent’s capability. AutoSearch Effectively Suppresses Over-Searching. Table[5.1](#S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3 "Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning") shows that Search-R1 and StepSearch exhibit high over-searching ratios, particularly on multi-hop tasks, indicating substantial redundant searches in prior methods. While HiPRAG reduces over-searching by leveraging external models, this comes at the cost of lower answer accuracy. In contrast, AutoSearch effectively suppresses over-searching while maintaining strong performance, leveraging the agent’s own capability to adaptively control search depth. *Table 3: Ablation study on search reward components in AutoSearch using Qwen2.5-3B base model.* | Method | General QA | | | | | | Multi-Hop QA | | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | NQ | | TriviaQA | | PopQA | | HotpotQA | | 2Wiki | | Bamboogle | | Avg | | | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | EM $\uparrow$ | SD $\downarrow$ | | \rowcolorblue!10Base model: Qwen2.5-3b-Base | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | AutoSearch | 43.7 | 1.03 | 61.7 | 1.05 | 46.0 | 1.07 | 39.4 | 1.49 | 41.6 | 1.69 | 33.1 | 1.83 | 44.3 | 1.36 | | w/o Base Reward | 40.4 | 1.36 | 57.7 | 1.37 | 44.2 | 1.38 | 34.2 | 1.79 | 37.2 | 2.02 | 31.2 | 2.02 | 40.8 | 1.66 | | w/o Search Efficiency Reward | 44.2 | 3.24 | 61.5 | 3.22 | 43.3 | 3.34 | 36.6 | 3.21 | 40.4 | 3.38 | 33.8 | 3.30 | 43.3 | 3.28 | | w/o Search Quality Reward | 40.2 | 1.01 | 58.6 | 1.03 | 42.9 | 1.01 | 33.2 | 1.09 | 36.1 | 1.22 | 30.8 | 1.25 | 40.3 | 1.10 | ### 5.3 Ablation Study We evaluate the contribution of the three reward mechanisms via ablation experiments on six QA datasets. Table[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning") shows that removing the base reward reduces accuracy and slightly increases search depth, highlighting its role in stabilizing the search process. Removing the search efficiency reward decreases accuracy and significantly increases search depth, indicating its importance for the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Removing the search quality reward lowers accuracy and noticeably reduces search depth, showing that it encourages more informative search steps. Overall, these results confirm that all three reward components are crucial for balancing answer accuracy and search efficiency. ### 5.4 Further Analysis Outcome-Based RL for AutoSearch. AutoSearch is primarily trained using step-wise rewards, which evaluate each search step. A natural question is whether outcome-based RL methods, such as GRPO, which optimize for final answer quality, can also be effective for AutoSearch. To investigate this, we treat AutoSearch’s cumulative reward as the outcome reward and apply GRPO for optimization. Figure[5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.4 Further Analysis ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning") compares the performance of AutoSearch trained with PPO versus GRPO. Surprisingly, GRPO achieves performance comparable to PPO, indicating the generality of AutoSearch. *Figure 5: The performance results(EM) of AutoSearch with PPO and GRPO on six datasets.* #### Training Dynamic of AutoSearch. As shown in Figure 6, we analyze the training dynamics of AutoSearch compared to Search-R1 and StepSearch. Search Time. Fig.[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Training Dynamic of AutoSearch. ‣ 5.4 Further Analysis ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning")(a) shows that while both Search-R1 and StepSearch initially reduce search time during early training, they later stabilize at relatively high values. In contrast, AutoSearch gradually decreases search time throughout training, achieving lower inference latency. Valid Actions Ratio. As illustrated in Fig.[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Training Dynamic of AutoSearch. ‣ 5.4 Further Analysis ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning")(b), all methods converge to valid actions. However, Search-R1 converges slowly, and StepSearch exhibits instability in later training. AutoSearch achieves the fastest convergence and maintains a high valid actions ratio, reflecting stable search. Search Depth. Fig.[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Training Dynamic of AutoSearch. ‣ 5.4 Further Analysis ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning")(c) shows that Search-R1 and StepSearch keep shallow search early but substantially increase search depth later. In contrast, AutoSearch briefly explores deeper search and then converges to a lower, stable depth, demonstrating higher efficiency. Token Length. As shown in Figure[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Training Dynamic of AutoSearch. ‣ 5.4 Further Analysis ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ Training and Evaluation ‣ Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ 4.4 RL Training ‣ 4.3 Search Quality Reward ‣ Search Efficiency Reward. ‣ Capability-aware Optimal Search Depth. ‣ 4.2 Search Efficiency Reward ‣ 4 Autosearch ‣ AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning")(d), Search-R1 and StepSearch initially generate short token length, but increases with deeper search, indicating higher resource consumption. In contrast, AutoSearch gradually reduces token length while maintaining accuracy, achieving a better balance between efficiency and answer quality. *Figure 6: Training dynamics of three models.*
